author: Trader Dale
title: Footprints Need Venue-Level Executed Volume
body: Centralized futures data lets the analyst observe executed size by price and side for that contract. Spot FX is decentralized, so a feed from one broker gives only a partial view of spot activity. Dale uses currency futures for analysis and maps the levels separately when executing in spot.

author: Trader Dale
title: Map Currency Futures Levels Before Spot Execution
body: Currency futures and spot pairs can use different quotation directions and price scales. Dale compares them side-by-side and uses an inverse display where appropriate. A corresponding swing or zone must be mapped to the execution instrument.

author: Trader Dale
title: Aggressive and Passive Orders Share Each Print
body: A market buy executes against a resting sell limit at the ask. A market sell executes against a resting buy limit at the bid. The print locates the transaction and its aggressive side, while the price response helps infer whether the passive side mattered.

author: Trader Dale
title: You Cannot Identify the Trader From the Print
body: A conspicuous ask-side execution could reflect buying initiative or the ability of a passive seller to absorb it. The number identifies the traded size, and the price response supplies separate information. Dale treats participant identity and intent as inferences.

author: Trader Dale
title: The Footprint Shows Executions at Each Price
body: A footprint keeps the candle's price range and layers executed bid and ask quantity onto each price row. This reveals where within the bar activity was concentrated. A normal candle only shows the aggregate price movement.

author: Trader Dale
title: A Footprint Node Is Its Busiest Price Row
body: Dale defines a bar's high-volume node by the largest combined bid and ask volume at a single price. This is a local, per-bar reference. A different time window can produce a different node.

author: Trader Dale
title: Bar Delta Is Executed Ask Minus Bid
body: Bar delta sums ask-side volume and subtracts bid-side volume across the footprint. A positive value indicates more buy-initiated execution, though the candle can still close lower. Rotations can make the relationship between delta and candle direction less reliable.

author: Trader Dale
title: Delta Can Diverge From Candle Direction
body: An up bar with negative delta or a down bar with positive delta shows price and executed aggression are telling different stories. Dale uses this discrepancy to investigate a reaction near a planned level. The example pairs an advancing price with weaker delta at resistance.

author: Trader Dale
title: Daily Profile Adds Context to a Footprint
body: Dale displays the day's volume distribution beside individual footprints to see where repeated trading took place. The daily histogram summarizes the session by price while the footprint shows how that activity was distributed within particular bars.

author: Trader Dale
title: Relative Volume Defines a Cluster
body: Dale's footprint shades rows based on executed size so unusually heavy areas stand out from nearby prices. A cluster is a band of relatively heavy trading. Interpretation depends on where the cluster forms and how price subsequently leaves it.

author: Trader Dale
title: Multiple Nodes Share One Price Across Bars
body: A double or triple node forms when the maximum-volume row repeats at the same price in successive footprints. A coincident level in separated bars is a different measurement. Dale treats this repetition as an area to watch when price returns.

author: Trader Dale
title: Footprint Imbalance Uses a Diagonal Comparison
body: Dale's default imbalance compares executions on one side with the opposing volume at the neighboring price and highlights ratios of 3 to 1 or higher. The diagonal convention differs from whether one side is larger within a single row. The software ratio is configurable.

author: Trader Dale
title: A Stack Groups Neighboring Same-Side Imbalances
body: Adjacent imbalance levels on the same side form a stack. Dale describes the usual display as three or more, while the trading instructions allow the configured trigger to vary. The stack highlights a band of unusually one-sided execution.

author: Trader Dale
title: Unfinished Business Is a Footprint-Extreme Test
body: Dale expects zero executed bid volume at a finished footprint high and zero executed ask volume at a finished low. He marks an extreme with prints on both sides as unfinished business. The mark is a level to track, and revisits can take time or fail to occur.

author: Trader Dale
title: Cumulative Delta Adds Signed Execution Over Time
body: Cumulative delta runs a sum of bar delta from the session start. Price and the running flow total can be shown on matching time axes to compare their direction. A different session reset changes the displayed series.

author: Trader Dale
title: Use Separate Views for Context and Confirmation
body: Dale's workspace pairs slower footprints for setup location with a faster footprint and a separate cumulative-delta view. The session profile gives a broader map for the same market. Each panel answers a different question about location or timing.

author: Trader Dale
title: Retest a Footprint Cluster Inside a Trend
body: Find relatively heavy trading inside a decisive directional leg, then observe whether price separates from the band. Dale waits for a pullback to its initial boundary or heavier portion. He aligns the setup with the direction of the leg.

author: Trader Dale
title: Defending Inventory Can Explain a Cluster Retest
body: Dale offers two explanations for a reaction at a prior cluster: earlier participants may defend their positions, and opposing traders may close as price approaches. Both are explanations for the observed reaction. The chart directly shows concentration, departure, return, and response.

author: Trader Dale
title: Profile the Cluster Inside a Sharp Rejection
body: Look for a fast move that reverses decisively, then locate relatively heavy trading inside the rejection. Track the band after price clearly leaves it and test the first return in the direction of rejection. The move can span more than one candle.

author: Trader Dale
title: Require Separation Before a Multiple-Node Retest
body: Dale looks for at least two consecutive bar nodes at the same price in a trend, pre-trend region, or strong rejection. His setup then waits for two entire footprints to form away from the node and considers its first later revisit. The approach determines the proposed side.

author: Trader Dale
title: A Large-Trade Filter Misses Split Execution
body: The filter highlights single executions above a configurable size. Dale's 25-lot illustration is calibrated to his currency-futures example, and activity varies by instrument and session. Small clips and iceberg replenishment can be missed by a large-print cutoff.

author: Trader Dale
title: Track Retests of Filtered Large Execution Areas
body: Identify a large execution with the trades filter, then wait for one or two entire footprints to build outside the marked area. Measure the first pullback to the zone after that separation. Dale uses the approach direction to distinguish support from resistance.

author: Trader Dale
title: Trade Stacked Imbalance Retests With Directional Context
body: A stack during a one-way move defines a candidate band. Dale waits for price to move away before it comes back and uses only the first test in this setup. A buying stack approached from above is considered possible support, and the mirrored case possible resistance.

author: Trader Dale
title: Treat Unfinished Business as a Nearby Reference
body: Dale uses an unfinished extreme in target planning, stop placement, and trade screening. Its presence can support a revisit hypothesis when price is already near it, but the market may first move far away. The reference alone gives no dependable entry timing.

author: Trader Dale
title: Check Unfinished Extremes Before Placing Stops
body: Dale checks whether a nearby unfinished extreme lies just beyond a proposed protective stop. The point is to understand whether a test of that extreme would also invalidate the chosen positioning. It remains secondary to the main setup and risk distance.

author: Trader Dale
title: Choose a Reference Before Reading Confirmation
body: Dale first identifies support or resistance with a primary method, then looks at order flow when price arrives. The four confirmation families are large passive orders, absorption, aggressive orders with delta, and cumulative-delta divergence. His presented confirmation setups depend on the location.

author: Trader Dale
title: Infer Passive Interest From a Stalled Extreme
body: At resistance a large ask print can accompany aggressive buying into a passive seller while price fails to extend. At support the mirrored example shows large bid volume during a stalled sell push. Unusually large is relative to the instrument and the session.

author: Trader Dale
title: Watch Heavy Two-Sided Volume Where Price Stalls
body: Dale's absorption setup looks for unusually heavy traded volume on both bid and ask around preselected support or resistance, while the previous push stalls. The evidence may take several minutes to appear. It is strongest as a response to a level already identified.

author: Trader Dale
title: Look for Aggression Away From the Reference
body: Dale watches for dominant bid-side execution and negative delta at resistance, or dominant ask-side execution and positive delta at support. He reads the response within five-minute footprints in these examples. The proposed aggression is in the direction of the reaction away from the level.

author: Trader Dale
title: Absorption and Initiative Form Different Stages
body: Dale describes a sequence in which passive interest first stalls a move and later aggressive traders push price away. The second stage supplies directional follow-through beyond the first stall. The footprint examples mark both stages separately.

author: Trader Dale
title: Read Cumulative-Delta Divergence Around Planned Levels
body: Dale's long example compares falling price with rising cumulative delta near support, with the mirror case near resistance. The mismatch is evaluated where the primary strategy already identified a meaningful zone. The hoped-for resolution belongs to the chart example and needs its own outcome test.

author: Trader Dale
title: Aim at the Near Edge of Prior Volume
body: When a trade approaches a zone with heavy historical activity, Dale considers taking profit before or at its leading edge. The zone may interrupt the move. A target selected from that distribution inherits the profile's window and price bins.

author: Trader Dale
title: Reassess a Trail When Order Flow Turns
body: Dale trails a favorable position while aggressive execution still supports the move. Opposing imbalance, renewed absorption, or a delta reversal near a significant price can change that read. The decision is conditioned on price location and progress.

author: Trader Dale
title: Place Stops Beyond the Price Structure
body: The book compares a fixed stop, a stop beyond the support or resistance extreme, and a stop beyond a heavy-volume band. The structural approaches tie the stop to the trade premise. Dale checks whether the resulting distance is sensible for the instrument and market conditions.

author: Trader Dale
title: Volume Profile Plots Executed Size by Price
body: A horizontal histogram bins executions by price across a selected interval. The thick portions show where more traded, whereas ordinary volume bars total activity by time interval. The profile identifies candidate price zones for further assessment.

author: Trader Dale
title: Profile Shape Describes Where Business Concentrated
body: Dale associates D with a broad middle distribution, P with a higher bulge, lowercase b with a lower bulge, and thin profiles with directional travel. Each shape summarizes where volume accumulated. The time window affects which shape is visible.

author: Trader Dale
title: Profile the Rotation Before a Directional Departure
body: Dale profiles the pre-move range and highlights its heaviest traded band once price breaks out. A later return to that band becomes a support or resistance candidate. The book pairs the return with a separate order-flow confirmation.

author: Trader Dale
title: Profile a Pause Within an Established Trend
body: A strong directional move can leave a thin distribution with a relatively large bump where it paused. Dale focuses on that local concentration for a potential continuation retest. The underlying trend and the actual response at the band are both part of his setup.

author: Trader Dale
title: Profile the Whole Rejection to Find the Fight
body: Apply a flexible profile over a strong rejected probe and its reversal to find the heaviest traded band inside the event. This can expose levels hidden by different candle time frames. Dale describes the method as harder to apply when several concentrations compete.
